item.dc:creator: Kayne, Richard
item.description:
Kayne, Richard · LingBuzz

As in Collins (2024), going back at least to Chomsky (1957), short passives must contain a syntactically merged (then deleted/silent) agent. In effect, the language faculty, in the spirit of Collins and Kayne (2023), does not allow for what might have been called ‘late insertion in the semantics’.

Like the better-studied pure exceptives introduced by ‘but’, ‘besides’ contributes an inference of exception when it occurs with quantifiers that exhibit universal force (e.g., ‘every’ or ‘no’). item.description:

The fact that impersonal transitive verbs can be passivised serves as a litmus test for any theory of passivisation. This results in situations of asymmetry in which certain grammatical distinctions made in the affirmative are unavailable in the negative. item.dc:creator: Kulkarni, Aaditya
item.description:
Kulkarni, Aaditya · LingBuzz

In this paper, I describe syntax and semantics of Marathi polar questions and polar questions particles to place them on the broader Indo-Aryan landscape. In doing so, I argue that Marathi polar question particles uniformly signal information-seeking polar questions when clause-final, while their clause-medial occurrences – wherever grammatical – signal non-canonical questions of various kinds. I show that this indicates a strict mapping between the syntactic and semantic-pragmatic notions of canonicity of questions and necessitates a closer examination of semantic-pragmatic properties of clause-medial polar question particles from Indo-Aryan languages previously described in the literature.
